entries.english: 81. The इ of इति is the single substitute for the अत् (of a word denoting imitation of an inarticulate sound) + इति ॥\nThe sound which is not distinct and clear, is called अव्यक्त ; when some one utters distinctly something which has some resemblance to that sound, by some contrivance, it is called अनुकरण or imitation of that sound. Thus पटत् + इति = पटिति ॥\nVārt:—This applies when the word consists of more than one syllable. Therefore it does not apply in the following :— श्रत् + इति = श्रदिति ॥
entries.note: Devanagari fragments reconstructed from Sanskrit commentary context; OCR misread 's of इति' corrected to 'इ of इति'.

entries.english: 82. This substitution does not take place when a sound-imitation word is doubled, here, however, for the final त् + of इति, the single substitute is optionally इ ( the second vowel ).\nVārtika:—There is diversely the repetition of the word when the affix डाच् follows.\nThe doubling takes place by this Vārtika. The word Āmredita is defined in the next sutra.
entries.note: Corrected OCR '&' to 'a', restored 'त्' from 'तू', fixed Ashtadhyayi reference reading.

entries.english: 83. Of that which is twice uttered, the latter word-form is called āmredita ( repeated ).\nThus पटत् पटत् + इति = पटत्पट + इ + ति = पटत्पटिति. Now, this para-rūpa rule is optional. The regular form therefore, will be without the elision of the final अत् as पटत् + पटत् + इति = पटत्पटदिति. The त् is changed to द् by the next sutra.
entries.note: Reconstructed heavily garbled Devanagari derivation steps from context.

entries.english: 84. A corresponding ज, ब, ग, ड or द is substituted for all consonants ( with the exception of semivowels and nasals) at the end of a word.\nAs वाग् अत्र, ‹?›, अग्निचिद् अत्र, त्रिवृद् अत्र ॥
entries.note: Spans pp. 55-56; garbled second example left as placeholder.

entries.english:
85. When a simple vowel is followed by a homogenous vowel, the corresponding long vowel is the single substitute for both the precedent and the subsequent vowels.
Thus दैत्य + अरिः = दैत्यारिः; श्री + ईशः = श्रीशः; विष्णु + उदयः = विष्णूदयः ॥ Why do we say " when a vowel follows " ? Observe कुमारी शेते. The word अच् is understood here also. The word सवर्णे, therefore, qualifies the word अच् understood. The rule will not apply if a homogenous consonant follows. As कुमारी शेते ॥ The ‹?› and ‹?› are homogenous, in spite of I. 1. 10: S. 13 for that prohibition does not apply to the long ई and because the rule of classification and inclusion contained in अणुदित्सवर्णस्य चाप्रत्ययः (I. 1. 69 S. 14 ) is not brought into operation at the time when नाज्झलौ (I. 1. 10) rule operates, because of its being a portion of सवर्ण rule. Therefore, so long as it does not come into operation it is not accomplished. Therefore first the rule of नाज्झलौ comes into play, then the rule of सवर्ण definition ( I. 1. 9 S. 10) and then comes the ग्राहकवाक्यम् ( I. 1. 69 S. 15). Therefore in नाज्झलौ those अच् only are taken which are not included in the class of homogenous vowels i. e. only the 9 vowels contained directly in अच्, and not the सवर्ण vowels which I. 1. 69 would have denoted. Therefore though short इ and ‹?› are not सवर्ण by I. 1. 10 the long ‹?› and ‹?› would be savarna. The sutra अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः would have been more clear if stated as अक्यकि ।
Why do we say 'an अक् or simple vowel ? Observe ‹?›. Why do we say by a homogenous vowel ?' Observe दधि + अत्र = दध्यत्र ॥
Vart:—When short ऋ is followed by short ऋ, the long substitution is optional so also with ऌ । This vartika is necessitated because ( 1 ) the two ऋ or the precedent and the subsequent ऋ are not homogenous, because one is samvrita and the other vivrita, or ( 2 ) because their prosodial length is 1½ and so the word दीर्घ cannot be applied with consistency in their case (ऌऌकार &c )
Or 3rdly (and this is the opinion of Bhattoji Dikshita) the single substitute short ऋ or short ऌ (which comes in the place of ऋ + ऋ or ऌ + ऌ) is really long consisting of two matras, in this way : होतृ + ऋकारः = होतृ + र् + ऋकारः ॥ These two र्'s are not visible in writing, but are there. They constitute one matra, for each consonant has half a matra. Thus one matra of two र्'s and one matra of ऋ make two matras really and though apparently short ऋ is retained, it is practically long. Similarly in the case of ऌ there are two ल्'s. In other words, the short ऋ (that comes in the place of two ऋ's) contains latent in it two र्'s, of one mātrā and its own self of one mātrā. Similarly the single substitute ऌ contains merged in it two ल्'s (of one matra ) and its own self of one matra.
Thus होतृ + ऋकारः = होतॄकारः or होतृकारः, so also होतृ + ऌकारः = होतॄकारः or होतऌकारः । The दीर्घ of ऌ is ‹?› ॥
Moreover, by the rule of ऋत्यकः VI. 1. 128. S. 92 the Sandhi is optional.
entries.note: Spans pp. 56-57; complex discussion with reconstructed grammatical references and placeholders for ambiguous Devanagari fragments.

entries.english: 86. In the room of ए or ओ final in a Pada, and the short अ, which follows it, is substituted the single vowel of the form of the first ( ए or ओ ) ॥\nThus हरे + अव = हरेऽव, विष्णो + अव = विष्णोऽव । This supersedes the substitutes अय् and अव् ॥
entries.note: Reconstructed missing vowels in heading and garbled Sanskrit examples.

entries.english: 87. After गो (when it retains the form गो and is final in a pada) the subsequent अ may optionally be retained everywhere, in the Vedas as well as in the secular literature.\nThus गो अग्रम् or गोऽग्रम् । Why do we say ending in an एङ् vowel ? Observe चित्रगु + अग्रम् = चित्रग्वग्रम् । Here गो does not end in ओ but has assumed the form उ and so the rule does not apply.\nWhy do we say at the end of a pada? Observe गोः ॥
entries.note: Reconstructed examples and grammatical markers from Sanskrit commentary context.
Entry cut off after Devanagari sutra line at bottom of page 57; English heading follows on page 58.

entries.english: 88. According to the opinion of Sphotayana, there is the substitution of ‹?› for the ‹?› of ‹?› when it is followed by any vowel. The anuvritti of ‹?› ceases, that of ‹?› manifests itself. Thus ‹?› + अथ = गवामम्, so also गवाजिनम्, गवोदनम्, गोष्ट्रम् or in the alternative we have गोऽग्रम्, गोऽजिनम्, गोऽदनम्, ‹?› ॥ The mention of Sphotayana is for the sake of respect, for the anuvritti of ‹?› was already understood in it. Why do we say final in a Pada? Observe ‹?›. This is a vyavasthita vibhasha, hence in ‹?› the substitution is compulsory and not optional.
entries.note: Devanagari sutra line absent from page 58 OCR (printed at foot of preceding page).

entries.english: 89. The substitution of ‹?› for the ओ of ‹?› is compulsory when the word ‹?› follows it. Thus गवेन्द्रः ॥ Note:— The Panini reads this sutra as ‹?›. Bhattoji has read the word nityam, in the next sûtra, instead of this.
entries.note: Panini reference digits in OCR read 6.1.125 instead of 6.1.124; embedded text reconstructed.

entries.english: 90. The Pluta (VIII. 2. 82 etc. S. 93) and Pragrihya (I. 1. 11 etc. S. 100.) vowels always remain unaltered when followed by a vowel (so far as the operation of that vowel is concerned). Thus एहिकृष्ण ३ भत्र गौश्चरति, हरी एतौ ॥ The force of the word nitya is that these pluta and pragrihya always retain their form and are not influenced by the rule of shortening given below. Thus in हरी ईशौ "The two Haris (Hari and Hara) are Lords," the present sûtra applies fully; for the long ई of हरी being Pragrihya, because it is the ‹?› of the dual number, retains its form. The subsequent rule does not apply, because ई is followed by a savarna letter, i.e. ई. In चक्री + अत्र = चक्री अत्र "The chakrin is here", the ई of चक्री is neither Pluta nor Pragrihya, because it is Nom. Singular, and therefore the subsequent rule of shortening fully applies to it, there being no scope for the application of any other rule. But in हरी + एतौ both the present sutra and the subsequent sutra find scope, and the subsequent sutra would make it हरि एतौ ॥ But the word nitya prevents this, and we have हरी एतौ ॥
entries.note: Panini reference digits in OCR read 9.1.125 instead of 6.1.125.

entries.english: 91. According to the opinion of Sakalya, the simple vowels with the exception of ṛ, when followed by a non-homogenous vowel, retain their original forms; and if the vowel is long, it is shortened. Thus चक्री + अत्र = चक्रि अत्र ‹?› The name of Sakalya is mentioned for the sake of respect. Because the alternative nature of this sutra is clear from its very formation. According to Mahabhashya, the च in the sutra is redundant. If it be said that च is necessary to draw the anuvritti of Prakriti-bhava, that is not the case. For the mere fact of making the long vowel short, shows that there is Prakriti-bhava. For if there were to take place Sandhi after shortening, as ‹?› + ‹?› = ‹?› = ‹?›, then where is the good of shortening, for the last form could have been obtained without shortening. Why do we say final in a Pada? Observe ‹?› ॥ Two Vart:— This rule of Sakalya is prohibited in the case of words which form invariable compounds (nitya samâsa) and of words formed by an affix having an indicatory ‹?› — Thus ‹?›. The word ‹?› is formed by a ‹?› affix, namely by ‹?› (V. 1. 106 S. 3495), added to ‹?› and therefore the ‹?› is changed to ‹?›. Before a ‹?› affix the previous word is considered a pada (I. 4. 16). Of nitya-compounds are वैयाकरण, सौवश्वः, व्याकरणं, कुमार्यम् which are so by II. 2. 18 S 761. Thus वाप्यश्वः is an example of compound; and formed by the affix ‹?› see I. 4. 16, S. 1252.
entries.note: Serial number misread as ६१ in OCR.

entries.english: 92. According to the opinion of Sakalya, the simple vowel followed by ‹?› retains its original form, and if the simple vowel is long, it is shortened. Thus ‹?› + ‹?› = ‹?› or ब्रह्मर्षिः ॥ The vowels must be final in a Pada here also, otherwise we have Sandhi as ‹?› + ‹?› = ‹?›. Even in compound this non-modification is observed, thus ‹?› or सप्तर्षीणाम् ॥ Why do we say when followed by ‹?›? Observe, ‹?› ॥ Why do we say "the simple vowels (अकः)"? Observe वृक्षावृश्यः (वृक्ष + ऋश्य) ॥ This rule applies even when the vowels are homogenous (which were excepted by the last rule), and it is not confined to ‹?› vowels as the last, but applies to ‹?› and ‹?› also.

93. Upto the close of this chapter (Second Pada of the Eighth Adhyâya), is always to be supplied: "the last vowel of a sentence is pluta and has the acute”. This is an adhikara sutra. All the three words i.e. "the last vowel"
entries.note: Entry cut off at bottom of page 60; serial number misread as ६३ in OCR.

entries.english: "(टि) of a sentence", "pluta" and "acute" are to be supplied in the subsequent aphorisms to complete the sense, up to the end of this Pada. Whatever we shall treat hereafter will refer to the final vowel (टि) in a sentence, and it will get the pluta lengthening and acute accent.

94. In answer to a salutation, but not when it refers to a Śūdra, the last vowel of a sentence becomes pluta and gets the acute accent.

The word अभिवादन means "respectful salutation of a superior or elder by an inferior or junior for the sake of obtaining his blessing. It consists of three acts 1. rising from the seat, 2. touching of the feet, 3. the uttering of the formula of salutation." The word प्रत्यभिवादन means, the blessing given by the superior or elder in answer to such salutation. In giving utterance to such blessing, the last vowel of the final word gets udātta and acute, provided that, such blessing not pronounced on a Śūdra.

Thus अभिवादये देवदत्तोऽहम् "I do salute you, I am Devadatta" is said by Devadatta to his Guru. The latter says भो आयुष्मान् एधि देवदत्त ३ ॥ "O Devadatta be thou long-lived"

Vārt:— Prohibition must be stated with regard to women also. As अभिवादये गार्ग्यहम् is said by Gārgī. To this the Guru replies:— भो आयुष्मती भव गार्गि ! ॥

Iṣṭi:—This prolation takes place there only, where the Proper Noun, Gotra &c. with which the salutation was made, is employed by the Guru at the end of the sentence; and not where the position of the Proper Name &c. is different. Therefore not here, देवदत्त कुशल्यसि ; देवदत्त आयुष्मान् एधि for here the word Devadatta is not used at the end of a sentence.

Vārt:—The prolation is optional, when भो follows such Proper Name, or when the Person addressed is a Kshatriya or a Vaishya. As अभिवादये देवदत्तोऽहं भोः ॥ Reply (1) आयुष्मान् एधि देवदत्त भोः ३ or (2) आयुष्मान् एधि देवदत्त भोः ॥ So also when a Kshatriya is addressed as अभिवादये इन्द्रवर्मन् भोः, Reply (1) आयुष्मान् एधि इन्द्रवर्म्मन् ३ or (2) आयुष्मान् एधि इन्द्रवर्म्मन् ॥ Vaishya: अभिवादये इन्द्रपालितोऽहं भोः ॥ Guru: आयुष्मान् एधि इन्द्रपालित ३ or आयुष्मान् एधि इन्द्रपालित ! ॥
entries.note: Reconstructed embedded Devanagari from Sanskrit commentary and context.

entries.english:
95. The final vowel of a sentence becomes pluta and acute, when used in calling a person from a distance.

The word ‹?› here includes, 'addressing in general', and not only 'calling'. Thus there is prolation here:— सक्तून् पिब देवदत्त ३ "O Devadatta! drink the gruel".
entries.note: Entry begins at bottom of page 61; English heading appears on page 62. Embedded example सक्तून् पिब देवदत्त ३ reconstructed.

entries.english:
96. When the words हे and है are employed, in addressing a person from a distance, there the हे and है alone get the pluta and the accent.

As हे ३ राम, or राम है ३ ॥
entries.note: Sutra number misread as EE; Panini ref digits corrected from 6.2.85 to 8.2.85; dropped Devanagari particles restored.

entries.english:
97. In the room of a prosodially long vowel, (with the exception of ‹?›) though it may not stand at the end, there is substituted a pluta for one at a time, under the above circumstances (of two previous Sutras,) in the opinion of Eastern Grammarians.

This sutra indicates a special sthânin for the pluta vowel taught by the two previous Sutras. With the exception of ‹?›, for every heavy vowel though it may not be the final vowel of the vocative word, and for the final vowel also, but only one at a time, there is pluta substitution, in the opinion of Eastern Grammarians. Thus दे ३ वदत्त or देव ३ दत्त or देवदत्त ३ ॥

Why do we say गुरोः "of a prosodially long vowel"? So that the ‹?› in Devadatta may not be prolated, for this is short.

Why do we say ‹?› "with the exception of ‹?›"? Observe ‹?› ॥

The word ‹?› shows that the prolation should not be simultaneous, but of one at a time; not ‹?› ॥

The word ‹?› "in the opinion of Eastern Grammarians" is used for the sake of creating option. So in one alternative, there is no prolation at all.
entries.note: Severely corrupted embedded Devanagari words and examples restored or replaced with ‹?›; ref digits normalized to 8.2.86.

entries.english:
98. Before the word इति in the Padapâtha, a Pluta vowel is treated like an ordinary apluta vowel.

The word उपस्थित means the affixing of इति in non-Rishi texts; i.e. when a Vedic text is split up into its various padas or words and इति is added. That is in Padapatha, the pluta is treated like an ordinary vowel, and hence there being no प्रकृतिभाव (VI. 1. 125), there is sandhi. Thus सुश्लोका ३ इति = सुश्लोकेति ॥ Why have we used the word वत् "like as"; instead of saying "the Pluta becomes Apluta" why do we say "Pluta is treated like apluta"?

By not using वत्, the whole Pluta itself would be changed into Apluta, and would give rise to the following incongruity. There is prakriti bhâva in the case of pluta and pragrihya. A vowel which is pluta need not be pragrihya, nor a pragrihya, a pluta. But where a vowel is both a pluta and a pragrihya at one and the same time, there will arise the difficulty. Thus in the dual अमी, the ई is pragrihya. It may be made pluta also as अमी ३ ॥ Now if before इति the pluta became apluta, then we shall not hear the prolation at all in अमी ३ इति formed by अमी ३ + इति ॥ For here the vowels will retain their form by being pragrihya by VI. 1. 125, S. 90, and in addition to that they will lose their pluta, by the present rule. But this is not intended. Hence the pluta is heard in अमी ३ इति ॥
entries.note: Embedded Devanagari reconstructed from Sanskrit commentary and context.

entries.english:
99. According to the opinion of Châkravarmaṇa, the pluta followed by a vowel is treated like an ordinary vowel.

Thus चिन्वन्ती ३ + इति = चिन्वन्तीति ॥ चिन्वन्ती ३ इति ॥ आगच्छ भो ३ इति ॥

The name of Châkravarmaṇa is used for the sake of making this an optional rule. This option applies to rule (VI. 1. 129, S. 98) as well as to words other than इति ॥

In the case of इति it allows sandhi optionally, when by the last rule there would have been always sandhi. In the case of words other than इति it ordains prakriti bhâva optionally, when there would have been always prakriti bhâva by VI. 1. 125, S. 90. This is a case of उभयत्र विभाषा, prâpta and aprâpta both.
entries.note: SK serial number misread as ९६ in Devanagari line; embedded Devanagari reconstructed from Sanskrit text.

entries.english:
100. A dual case affix ending in ई or ऊ or ए is called Pragrihya, or excepted vowels which do not admit of sandhi or conjunction.
As a general rule, Sanskrit allows of no hiatus in a sentence. If a word ends in a vowel, and the next word begins with a vowel, the two vowels coalesce, according to certain rules. This is called sandhi. But pragrihyas are exceptions to this sandhi, "they are certain terminations, the final vowels of which are not liable to any sandhi rules." This sutra gives three of these terminations, viz., the duals of nouns or verbs ending in ई (ईत्), ऊ (ऊत्), or ए (एत्) ॥ Thus :— हरी एतौ; विष्णू इमौ; गङ्गे अमू. Here according to the general rule of sandhi, the final ई of हरी and the initial ए of एतौ ought to have coalesced into an ऐ, but it is not so, because हरी is the nominative dual of हरि.
Vart:—The prohibition of इव &c., should be stated in treating of the pragrihya nature of ई, ऊ &c. Thus मणी (two gems) + इव = मणीव "like two gems". So also दम्पतीव "like a couple", जम्पतीव "like man and wife," रोदसीव "like heaven and earth." Some say that this vartika is unnecessary. Because the final member of the above words is not इव, but the particle वा only, which has the same meaning as iva.
entries.note: Reconstructed embedded Devanagari in heading and commentary from clear context.

entries.english:
101. (The long ई and ऊ) after the म of the pronoun अदस् are Pragrihya.
In the pronoun अदस् the dual termination in ई, ऊ or ए will be pragrihya by force of the last sûtra, but the present sûtra makes this addition, that in the case of all terminations ending in ई, or ऊ and preceded by म, of whatever number they may be, will be pragrihya. As a matter of fact, there are only two such terminations satisfying the above conditions, namely ई and ऊ. The rule may therefore be put in the following words:—"The terminations of ‹?› nom. plur. masc. and nom. dual of the pronoun अदस् are pragrihya." As अमी ईशाः । रामकृष्णावमू आसाते । There is no example of the word adas ending in ए.
Why do we say "after the letter म"? Because in the example अमुके + अत्र = अमुकेऽत्र, the ए, preceded not by a म but by the क of अकच् (V. 3. 71, S. 2026) is not pragrihya, which it would have been by the influence of the last sûtra which includes ए as well as ई and ऊ, and from which the word dual is not supplied here, else this rule would be useless.
entries.note: Reconstructed embedded Devanagari from context; uncertain word 'Brand' left as placeholder.

entries.english:
102. The affix शे, (the Vedic substitute of the case-affixes), is a pragrihya.
In the Vedic Sanskrit, the declension of nouns sometimes differs somewhat from the ordinary Sanskrit. One of the peculiar Vedic terminations, which replace the ordinary declensional terminations is called शे (VII. 1. 39, S. 3561). Thus अस्मे इन्द्राबृहस्पती ॥
Of this substitute शे, the initial श is indicatory, the real suffix being ए. This final ए is a pragrihya.
entries.note: Corrected misread Devanagari characters in heading and text.

entries.english:
103. A particle consisting of a single vowel, with the exception of the particle आङ् is a Pragrihya.
All such particles technically called nipâta which consist of a simple vowel without any consonant, are pragrihya and therefore are not liable to the rules of sandhi. As इ इन्द्रः has the sense of wonder, उ उमेशः, उ has the sense of a doubtful question.
आङ् which is not a pragrihya, has four significations:—(1) As a diminutive particle when joined to adjectives and nouns, आ + उष्णम् = ओष्णम् (2) as a prefix to verbs, it expresses the senses of "near", "near to", and with verbs of "motion", "taking" &c., it shows the reverse of the action, as गम, 'to go', आगम, 'to come', आ + इहि = एहि, (3) as showing the limit inceptive (अभिविधि) "from", "ever since", as आजन्मनः "ever since his birth", (4) as showing the limit exclusive (मर्यादा), "till", "until", as आ + अध्ययनात् = आऽध्ययनात् "until the reading begins". When the particle आ has not any one of the above four senses and is used in expressing regret &c., it is a pragrihya, as आ एवं किलासीत् "Ah! such there once was", आ एवं मन्यसे "Oh! do you think so."
entries.note: Corrected garbled Devanagari examples in commentary.

entries.english:
104. The final ओ of a particle is a pragrihya.
As अहो ईशाः ॥

105. The final ओ of the vocative singular before the word इति according to Śâkalya, in secular or non-Vedic literature, is pragrihya.
This sûtra gives the opinion of the Rishi Śâkalya, so that it is an optional rule. Thus the forms above given are correct.
In ârsha literature the sandhi is imperative, not optional, as एता गा ब्रह्मबन्धवेत्यब्रवीत् ॥

106. The particle उञ् before इति, according to Śâkalya is a Pragrihya.
This sûtra consists of the single word उञ् meaning उ. This is also an optional rule. Thus उ इति or विति ॥
entries.note: Corrected garbled Devanagari in heading and text.

entries.english:
107. The particle ॐ replaces उञ् in non-Vedic literature, and it is a pragrihya in the opinion of Śâkalya.
Before the word इति the word उञ् is replaced sometimes by ॐ the long nasal उ. ॐ + इति = ॐ इति or विति ॥
entries.note: Corrected OCR misreads of Devanagari in heading and text.

entries.english:
108. व् is optionally the substitute of the particle उञ्, when it is preceded by a मय् consonant (all consonants with the exception of semivowels, sibilants, and ह), and is followed by a vowel.
Thus kimu uktam or kimvuktam. The उ is a Pragrihya and therefore would have remained unchanged, this ordains व् optionally. This being considered asiddha, the म् is not changed to anusvâra in the above example.
entries.note: Restored missing and misread Devanagari in heading and commentary.

entries.english: When this is followed by इति, and preceded by a consonant, then by I. 1. 17, S 106 it is optionally ‹?›, and it may be replaced by It. When it is not a pragrihya, then it is changed to ‹?› by (VI. 1. 77, S 47), or to ‹?› by the present sûtra. In the case of ‹?›, there is anusvâra by VIII. 3. 23, S 122 as ‹?›. When it is a Pragrihya, then it is changed to ‹?› by the present sûtra as ‹?›. So also with substitute, where the ‹?› will be nasal: as किमिति, or ‹?› will remain unchanged, as किम उँ इति. Thus we have five forms with इति ॥
entries.note: Tail fragment continued from previous batch.

entries.english:
109. The final ई and ऊ of words giving the sense of the locative case are pragrihya.

This sûtra finds its scope in the Vedic literature generally. There is a sûtra (VII. 1. 39, S. 3561) which declares that "in the Vedic Sanskrit, the case-affixes sup are often replaced either by ‹?› or are altogether elided, or they are changed into a letter homogeneous with the prior letter, or ‹?›, or ‹?›, or ‹?›, or ‹?›, or ‹?›, or ‹?›, or ‹?› takes their place." Let us take the example where a case-affix is changed into a letter homogeneous with the prior. Thus the case-affix of the seventh case is ‹?› (1). In forming the L. S. of "body," we have तनू + ‹?›. The ‹?› will be changed into a homogeneous letter with ऊ and we have तनू + ऊ = तनू "in the body," as, मध्यस्थां मामकीतनू (for ‹?›). This is the Vedic form, the secular form being तनूयाम्. Similarly गौरी + इ = गौरी "on the Gauri," as सोमो गौरी अधिश्रितः (Rig Veda IX, 12, 3). It is in such cases, therefore, that the long ई and ऊ are used in the sense of locative, and are pragṛihya.

It is only long ई and ऊ which are pragrihya, and not any other vowel, though used in the sense of locative. Thus by the same aphorism (VII. 1. 39) dâ (डा) may be employed to denote the seventh case-affix. Thus अग्ने + ‹?› = अश्मा + डा = अश्मा 'in the fire,' as, प्रियः सूर्ये प्रियो अश्मा भवाति व इंद्राय सुतोमो दाश (Rig Veda V. 37. 5). Here though in the locative case, its final is not pragrihya. Therefore अश्मा + इति = अश्मेति ॥

The ई and ऊ must be of the 7th case. Therefore मती + ‹?› (3rd. s.) = मती (letter homogeneous with the prior) 'with wisdom.' Here मती is in the sense of the instrumental case and is not pragrihya. Thus मती + इति = मतीति ॥

The word अर्थे is used in the aphorism, in order to exclude the application of this rule to cases like the following. Thus in forming the compound of वाप्याम् "in the well" and अश्वः "horse," the case-affix is elided, and we get वाप्यश्वः. Here, no doubt, the word वापी is in the locative case, though the case-affix is elided; but we cannot say that the long ई of vapi has the sense of the locative. Here, therefore, we shall have sandhi; as, वाप्यश्वः "the horse near the well."

In other words, the present aphorism is not to apply to the final ई or ऊ of words standing as the prior member of a compound term (pûrva-pada); for words like वापी &c., in the above example, can never, by themselves and alone, denote the locative case; while words like तनू, formed in the way described already, give the sense of the locative, even alone, though they be placed anywhere in a sentence.
entries.note: Devanagari serial number misprinted as 106 in scan; fixed to 109 following English heading and sequence.

entries.english:
110. The anunâsika is optionally the substitute of an vowel which occurs in a Pause, and is not a Pragrihya.

अ, इ, and उ, short and long, may, when final in a Pause, be pronounced as nasals, provided that they are not Pragrihya. The अण् is a Pratyâhâra with the first ण. Thus दधीँ or दधि.

Why do we say 'which is not a pragrihya'? Observe अग्नी इति.

111. The letter स and the dental when coming in contact with श and the palatals, are changed to श and palatals respectively.

1st. स in contact with श: as, हरिस् + शेते = हरिशेते.
2nd. स in contact with चु:—as, रामस् + चिनोति = रामश्चिनोति.
3rd. तु with श:—अग्निचित् + शेते = अग्निचिच्छेते. So सोमसुच्छेते ॥
4th. तु with चु:—सत् + चित् = सच्चित्.
5th. झकार followed by तकार; as, यज् + न (III. 3. 90, S 3268) = यज् + ञ = यज्ञः, याच् + न = याज्ञा ॥

In fact the instrumental case श्चुना shows that the mere contact of स् and तु with श and चु is enough to induce the change, whether स्तु is followed by चु, or चु be followed by स्तु ॥ Other examples of mere contact are:—

5th. (a) श followed by त is changed into श: as, भ्रस्ज् + ति = ‹?› (III. 1. 77, S 2534; VI. 1. 16, S 2412) = ‹?› (VIII. 4. 53, S 52) = भृज्जति ॥ Similarly मस्ज् forms मज्जति, व्रश्च् forms वृश्चति ॥

The next aphorism शात् (VIII. 4. 44, S. 112) which prohibits the change of तु into चु when following the letter श, indicates by implication that the rule of mutual correspondence according to the order of enumeration (I. 3. 10, S 128) does not hold good here.

Had the sûtra been स्तोः श्चोः i.e. instead of instrumental, had there been the locative case, then the rule would not have applied to cases covered by the fifth clause.

112. In the room of तु there is not a palatal substitute, when श precedes.

The words न and स्तोः are understood here. This is an exception to
entries.note: Text cut off at page boundary.

entries.english:
...the last rule. Thus विछ् + न (III. 3. 90. S. 3268) = विश् + न (VI. 4. 19. S. 2561) = विश्नः ॥
Similarly प्रश्नः ॥

113. The letters स् and dentals in contact with ष् and cerebrals, are changed into ष् and cerebrals respectively.
The word स्तोः is to be read into the sûtra. Here also there is absence of mutual correspondence according to the order of enumeration.
(1) स् with ष्, as, रामस् + षष्ठः = रामष्षष्ठः ॥
(2) स् with ट्, as, रामस् + टीकते = रामष्टीकते ॥
(3) त् with ष्, as, पेष् + ता = पेष्टा ॥
(4) त् with ट्, as, तत् + टीका = तट्टीका ॥ चक्रिन् + ढौकसे = चक्रिण्ढौकसे ॥

114. After a cerebral (टोः) final in a Pada, the change of a dental (स्तु) to a cerebral (ष्टु), does not take place, except in the case of the affix नाम् ॥
Thus षट् + सन्तः = षट्सन्तः ॥ षट् + ते = षट्ते ॥
Why do we say पदान्तात् 'final in a Pada'? Observe ईड् + से = ईड् + टे = ईट्टे ॥
Why do we say टोः 'after a cerebral (टु)'? Observe सर्पिष् + तमम् = सर्पिष्टमम् ॥
Why do we say अनाम् 'except in the case of the affix nâm'? Observe षट् + नाम् = षण्णाम् ॥ This exception is very inadequate. Hence the following Vârtika: it should be stated rather that नवति and नगरी as well as नाम are not prevented from undergoing the cerebral change. As, षण्णाम् 'of six', षण्णवतिः ninety-six, षण्णगर्यः six cities.
entries.note: Restored OCR-corrupted Devanagari words and fixed fragmented/misplaced example line

entries.english:
115. In the room of a dental (तु), there is not a cerebral substitute, when ष follows.
The word न is to be read into the aphorism. As, सन् + षष्ठः = सन्षष्ठः ॥
Here the Sûtra झलां जशोऽन्ते (S. 84) should be read again, by which a soft consonant is substituted for the hard. Thus वाक् + ईशः = वागीशः ; चित् + रूपम् = चिद्रूपम् ॥

116. In the room of a यर letter (every consonant except ह) final in a Pada, when a Nasal follows, there is optionally a Nasal substitute.
The word पदान्त is understood here. Thus एतत् + मुरारिः = एतन्मुरारिः or एतद्मुरारिः । This rule does not apply to र्, as चतुर् + मुखः = चतुर्मुखः ॥
Why do we say 'final in a Pada'? Observe, वेद् + मि = वेद्मि ॥ Here there is no option. So also ‹?› ॥
Vart:—When it is a pratyaya or affix that follows, the nasalisation is obligatory in the secular language. Thus तत् + मात्रम् = तन्मात्रम्, similarly चिन्मयम् ॥ It is, however, only before the affixes मात्र and मयट् that the change is obligatory, and not before every affix beginning with a nasal.
How do you explain the form ककुद्मन्तः in the sentence 'महोक्षाः ककुद्मन्तः'? Because the द is used in यवादि class (For a list of the words belonging to this class, see Ganapatha VIII. 2. 9).
entries.note: Unclear OCR token 'guaifa' replaced with placeholder; restored missing Devanagari letters in Vartika explanation

entries.english:
117. In the room of तु (a dental) when the letter ल follows, one homogeneous with the latter is substituted.
Thus तत् + लयः = तल्लयः ; विद्वान् + लिखति = विद्वाँल्लिखति ॥ Here त् has been changed to pure ल्, while the dento-nasal न् is changed to a nasal लँ.

118. After उद्, in the room of the स of sthâ and stambha, the substitute is a letter belonging to the class of the prior (i.e. a dental is substituted for this स) |
As उद् + स्थाता = उद् + स्थाता = उद् + थाता (VIII. 4. 63 S. 120) = उत् + थाता (VIII. 4. 55 S. 121) = उत्थाता, उत्थातुम्, उत्थातव्यम् ॥ So also with स्तम्भ, as, उत्तम्भिता, उत्तम्भितुम् &c. (See I. 1. 67 S. 41 and 54. S. 44)
Here the Aghoṣa (Surd) and Mahâprâṇa स is changed to थ which is also Aghoṣa and Mahâprâṇa. This थ then is optionally elided by झरो झरि (S. 71). But in the alternative when there is no lopa the थ् is heard in pronunciation.
By the rule खरि च (S. 121), the थ् is not changed to चर् letter, because the rule of चर् is not applicable to थ्; for this थ् is considered as non-existent for the purposes of चर् rules.
entries.note: Extensive Devanagari character repair across page break (थ/थ् misread as यू, चर् misread as घर/वर)

entries.english:
119. In the room of the letter ह, after झय् (a sonant Mute) there is optionally a letter homogeneous with the prior.
The pratyâhâra झय् includes all Mutes. But practically sonant Mutes are only taken here. The substitute of ह् will be घ् by the rule of nearness of place of utterance, because ह् is a ghoṣa (sonant); Mahâprâṇa (aspirated) and Saṁvṛta (contracted) and so is also घ्. Thus वाक् + हरिः = वाग्घरिः or वाग्हरिः ॥
entries.note: Restored corrupted Devanagari letters in explanation and examples

entries.english:
120. In the room of a श् preceded by a surd Mute, there is optionally the letter छ when a vowel or ह, य, व or र follows such a श् ॥
Though झय् means all Mutes, the rule, however, applies to surd mutes. The words झय् and अन्यतरस्याम् are to be read into the sûtra. Thus तत् + शिव = तद् + शिव (S. 84) = तद् + छिव = तच् + छिव = तच्छिव. At this stage applies the next Sûtra.
entries.note: Restored OCR-corrupted Devanagari characters in rules and phonetic condition

entries.english:
121. In the room of झल्, there is the substitute चर् when खर् follows.
A sonant non-aspirate mute is the substitute of a mute, when a surd mute or a sibilant follows. The words झलाम् and चरः are supplied from the last sûtra. Therefore ‹?› is changed to ‹?› and we have the form ‹?› or ‹?› :
entries.note: Entry truncated at page end; embedded Devanagari corrupted

entries.english:
Vārtika:—It should rather be stated when a letter of अम् pratyāhāra follows. The sūtra only gives अट् letters, the Vārtika adds the letters ल्, and the nasals.
Thus तत् + श्लोकेन = ‹?›.
Why do we say when a letter of pratyāhāra follows? Observe ‹?›.
entries.note: Tail continuation from preceding page; embedded Devanagari fragments damaged in scan.

entries.english:
122. The Anusvāra is substituted for म्, at the end of a word, before a consonant.
Thus हरिवन्दे ॥ The word हलि is understood in this sūtra. The म् must be at the end of a pada which we get from sūtra अलोऽन्त्यस्य (S. 42); therefore not here: गम्यते.
entries.note: Restored missing 'म्' after 'for' and before 'must be' based on context.

entries.english:
123. The Anusvāra is substituted for the न् and म्, not final in a pada, before all consonants, with the exception of Nasals and semi-vowels.
Thus यशांसि, आक्रंस्यते ।
Why do we say before a झल् consonant? See मन्यते.
Note:—Why do we say 'not final in a Pada'? Observe राजन् पाहि.
entries.note: Corrected OCR misreads of Devanagari characters in English context (स -> झल्, मम्यते -> मन्यते).

entries.english:
124. In the room of anusvāra, when यय् follows, a letter homogeneous with the latter is substituted.
Thus अङ्कितः, अञ्चितः, कुण्ठितः, शान्तः, शुम्फितः. These are thus formed:—
To the causal churādi root अङ्कि (meaning pada and lakshaṇa), we add the participial affix क्त. Thus अङ्कि + क्त. The causal sign is elided by the sūtra ‹?› (VI. 4. 52. S. 3057). Then by the present rule, we have ‹?›. The इ here is the इट् augment. Or it may be from the root अकि (meaning lakshaṇa) where the augment नुम् becomes anusvāra by VIII. 3. 24, S. 123, and then this न् becomes ङ्.
अञ्चितः comes from the root अञ्चु (meaning pūjā), with the affix क्त. The न् is not elided by VI. 4. 30 S. 424.
कुण्ठितः is formed from the root कुष्ठि (meaning pratighāta). The augment नुम् is added to the root before the सेट् participial affix. This is changed into ण्.
शान्तः is formed from the root शम् (meaning upaśama) with the affix क्त (See VII. 2. 27. S. 3068). The अ of शम् is lengthened by VI. 4. 15. S. 2666. The म् is changed to न् by the present rule.
शुम्फितः is formed from the root शुम्भू (meaning grantha) with the affix क्त. In कुर्वन्ति, the न is not changed into ण, though required by VIII. 4. 3. S. 197. Because the ‹?› is asiddha, and therefore by the prior rule VIII. 3. 24. S. 123, the न् is first changed into anusvāra (VIII. 2. 1. S. 12). That anusvāra is again changed into न by the present rule, न being homogeneous with त्. This change again being असिद्ध as if it had never taken place (VIII. 2. 1. S. 12), the ण is never substituted for न ॥
entries.note: Entry spans pages 73-74; repaired multiple OCR corruptions in grammatical derivations.

entries.english:
125. In the room of anusvāra final in a Pada, the substitution of a letter homogeneous with the latter is optional.
Thus त्वङ्करोषि or त्वं करोषि; संय्यन्ता or संयन्ता; संव्वत्सरः or संवत्सरः; यँल्लोकम् or यं लोकम्.
Here the anusvāra has become nasal य् व् ल् in the other alternative.

126. म् is substituted for the म् of सम्, before the word राज् ending with the affix क्विप् ॥
Thus सम्राट् ॥
The substitution of म for म is for the sake of preventing the anusvāra change (VII. 1. 40. S. 3562.). Why do we say 'before राज्'? See संव्राट् (VI. 4. 40. S. 2986. Vārt). Why do we say 'of सम्'? Observe विट् राह (V. 4. 70 S. 955). Why do we say 'ending with क्विप्'? Observe संराजिता, संराजितुम्, संराजितव्यम् ॥
The क्विप् is added by III. 2. 61 S. 2975; the ज् is changed to ष् by VIII. 2. 36, S. 294, which is changed to ड् at the end of a word, in सम्राट् ॥ साम्राज्यम् is formed by ष्यञ् affix, as it belongs to Brāhmaṇādi class.
entries.note: Heading restored dropped 'म्'; repaired OCR corruptions in derivation explanation.

entries.english:
127. म is optionally substituted for म् before that ह which itself is followed by a म ॥
The म् may be changed to anusvāra or remain unchanged before a word beginning with ‹?›. Thus for किम् ह्मलयति, 'what does he cause to shake'?
Vārt:—Before ‹?›, ‹?› and ‹?›, the preceding ‹?› may be changed to य, व or ल respectively.
Now, by this Vārtika, three letters य्, व्, ल्, are ordained in the room of ‹?›. But the rule does not say which letter is to be substituted for which letter. To remove this doubt the following interpretation sūtra should be remembered:—
entries.note: Spans pages 74-75; corrected OCR artifacts in English prose and preserved illegible Devanagari with placeholders.

entries.english:
128. When a rule involves the case of equal numbers of substitutes and of things for which these are to be substituted, their mutual correspondence or assignment of each to each, is according to the order of enumeration.
Therefore as under the former rule, the letters to be substituted are three in number and the substitutes are also three in number, therefore applying the present rule, ‹?› would be replaced by ‹?›; ‹?› by ‹?› and ‹?› by ‹?›. Thus we have किं ह्यः or किं ह्यः; किं ह्वलयति or किं ह्वलयति; किं ह्लादयति or किं ह्लादयति.

129. न् is optionally substituted for म्, when it is followed by ह which has a न् after it.
म् becomes न् before a word beginning with ह्; as किन्नुते or किं ह्नुते ॥
entries.note: Corrected OCR misreads of Devanagari characters in English context ('स' -> 'म्', 'ऋ' -> 'ह').

entries.english:
130. The augment कुक् is added to a final ङ्, and the augment टुक् to a final ण्, before a sibilant, optionally.
The कुक् and टुक् augments being considered as asiddha, there is no change, i.e. soft letters are not substituted for the hard. Before giving
